Moreover, he could have withdrawn his motion, thereby saving many Liberals and C.C.F. members from voting against their own actual wish for a national flag.

(Text):

maintopic: MR. ROBICHAUD    REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
MR. ROBICHAUD    REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege based on an editorial which appears this day, November 28, 1957, in a daily newspaper and which concerns all members of this parliament as well as members of previous parliaments. In the Montreal Gazette of this date the following editorial appears: Christmas Cards And All That
Thousands of Canadians this year will not be receiving the Christmas cards they had from Ottawa in other years. The reason they may not be receiving them is quite simple: they will no longer be paying for them.
It seemed, for the time being, rather pleasant to have Yule greetings from your member of parliament. It showed that he had not forgotten you. He had even gone so far as to send you his greetings and his best wishes-for Christmas and the New Year, and all that.
But the unpleasant thing about these pleasant greetings is that you had to pay to be greeted. And you paid nonetheless because you never actually saw the bill. It was still charged to your account, in the taxation you paid.
This year there will be no Christmas cards for members of parliament, provided by the courtesy of those to whom they were to be sent. The estimated saving is $50,000.
Perhaps there may be some elector somewhere anxiously waiting for his member's card. But it may be doubted. That $50,000 saving will be quite a compensation for not being greeted with your own money.
But perhaps the happiest electors of all may be those who helped pay for these cards but never even got one. They are now being forgotten at less cost to themselves.
The point of my question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is that this editorial leaves the impression the members of parliament were in the past supplied with free Christmas cards which they were sending out to their respective constituents. This is absolutely false, and the newspaper responsible for such an irresponsible and untrue statement should apologize to this parliament and to the people of this country for misinforming them. Furthermore, most members of this house present and past paid for the postage used on their Christmas cards and did not take advantage of the privilege of the frank to which they were entitled.

Inquiries of the Ministry member for Vancouver East addressed this question to me, and I took it as notice:
Has the interdepartmental committee which we were informed last session was being set up reported to the government the position Canada should take on the legal position of the continental shelf and territorial waters in its representations to the international conference which the general assembly of the United Nations recommended should be held in March, 1958? If so, is it the minister's intention to make the government's views known to the House of Commons, and will provision be made for a discussion on this allimportant subject?
The answer is that the interdepartmental committee, which is making preparations for Canada's participation in the international conference on the law of the sea, which is to be held in Geneva commencing February 24, 1958, has not yet completed drafting its recommendations to the government on all the matters which will be discussed at the conference. The basis of the discussion at the conference will be a report of the international law commission of the general assembly incorporating some 73 recommendations on the various aspects of the law of the sea: territorial waters, continental shelf, navigation, fishing and so on.
The interdepartmental committee has, however, made recommendations to the government on some of the more important aspects of the international law commission's report, among these the questions of the territorial sea and the continental shelf, as a result of an invitation addressed to governments by the Secretary General of the United Nations for comments on the international law commission's report.
It is the secretary general's intention to include the comments he receives from member governments in documentation being prepared by the secretariat of the United Nations for the conference.
Provisional comments of the government were forwarded to the secretary general on September 10 last. I would draw attention to the fact that they are provisional comments, Mr. Speaker. These may be modified in view of the discussions to be held at the conference, and having regard to the negotiations that might take place at that time among the nations.
Since these comments will be of general interest I would ask leave of the house to have the note which was sent to the secretary general printed as an appendix to Hansard. This note is six pages long and it is single spaced. To discuss at this time the whole range of matters which will be taken up at the international conference would, I think, be premature. However, the house will now be acquainted with the views which

Inquiries of the Ministry have been put forward by the government on some of the more important aspects of these matters.

subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 4, to provide for minimum wages for employees.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before I address myself directly to the motion for the second reading of this bill may I say a word as to my own intentions today, in view of the fact that a number of the public bills on the order paper are in my name. This is the only Thursday we shall have this session for public bills, in other words bills regarding public matters brought forward by private members. If the consideration of this bill were completed it would be unfair on my part if I were to ask the house to take the rest of the day dealing with another of my bills. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope the house will not take too long on this bill but that a decision can be reached-naturally I hope it will be a favourable decision-and that having been accomplished, I should like

the rest of my bills in this first group to stand so that other members with bills on the order paper might also have a chance to present their bills to the house this day.
In keeping with what I have just said I shall endeavour to speak as briefly as I can in support of Bill No. 4. To put it in a nutshell, the purpose of this bill is to establish a minimum rate of wages with respect to all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction.
This bill provides that such minimum rate of wages shall be $1 per hour. The bill also provides that its terms do not affect any employee whose rate of wages is higher than the minimum established by this legislation. However, any rate of wages less favourable to employees than $1 per hour is superseded by this bill.
With one exception, Mr. Speaker, I believe this is the only occasion in the history of the Canadian parliament when a bill has been presented proposing a minimum wage law for Canada. That single exception was, of course, in 1935, when the government of the late Mr. Bennett, who was prime minister at that time, presented to parliament what was popularly known as the Bennett new deal legislation. Parliament in that session before the 1935 election passed chapter 44 of the statutes of Canada for that year, which was known as the minimum wages act. However, that act, along with several other pieces of that Bennett new-deal legislation, was declared ultra vires of the powers of the federal parliament when it was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada by the Liberal government that came into office after the election of 1935.
The reason that act was ruled ultra vires was that it had been established by the courts by that time that labour matters come in part under federal jurisdiction but in part under provincial jurisdiction. Therefore it was not competent for the federal parliament to pass one minimum wages act applying to all workers in Canada. I think it is fair to say that Mr. Bennett, the eminent lawyer that he was, knew of this difficulty and he tried to meet it by a rather lengthy and interesting preamble which can be found in chapter 44 of the statutes of 1935. The gist of that preamble was that Canada, having agreed to an international convention regarding the establishment of certain labour standards, including minimum wages, was obligated by that treaty arrangement to put such legislation on the statute books of the country. Nevertheless that position did not stand up when the minimum wages act of 1935 was taken to the supreme court. So far as I can ascertain, from that day to this parliament has not had occasion to debate an
Industrial Relations
actual bill for the enactment of a minimum rate of wages so far as the federal parliament is concerned.
The bill now before us, Mr. Speaker, clearly avoids the error of Mr. Bennett's bill of 1935. The bill now before us, like the two bills respecting annual vacations with pay now on the order paper, like the fair employment practices act and like the act providing for equal pay for equal work, makes it clear that it covers only those employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction. Not only have we in the federal parliament the right to legislate regarding employees in those works and undertakings that come under federal labour jurisdiction but some of us feel that we have the duty and obligation to do so. In other words, just as v/e have already enacted the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and these other pieces of legislation to which I have referred, some of us feel that the so-called labour code at the federal level should be rounded out and that we should make provision for such things as annual vacations with pay, statutory holidays with pay, minimum rates of wages, maximum hours of labour and so on for all those workers who are not protected by provincial legislation but who come under federal labour jurisdiction.
I say that this is the first time since 1935 that the house has had a chance to debate this issue. It is, of course, not the first time that this suggestion has been made on the floor of parliament. Some of us have been doing that for a long time, as we have been arguing for uniform labour standards across Canada. In addition, I might point out that this bill has been introduced and given first reading in parliament previous to this session but this is the first time that it has actually been reached for debate on second reading.
We in this group who present this bill to parliament are not alone in our support of the idea that there should be this kind of legislation providing for a minimum rate of wages for all employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction. The point, of course, was made very effectively once again this year in the submission made by the Canadian Labour Congress to the new government on October 21, 1957. Most of us remember that very interesting occasion in the railway committee room when the Canadian Labour Congress, only a week after parliament had met, appeared before the government at which time Mr. Jodoin read this brief and at which time the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) replied on behalf of the government.
One of the points that is underlined in the brief is that in filling out the gaps in labour

Industrial Relations
legislation there should be legislation providing for a minimum rate of wages for employees who come under federal jurisdiction. The Canadian Labour Congress says this about it on page 18 of its brief:
But the dominion should not confine itself to doing as well as the best of the provinces. It should give a lead. It should, specifically, establish a legal maximum work week of 40 hours and a legal maximum wage of $1 an hour. This is not really a very drastic proposal.
After some references to the maximum work week the brief goes on to say:
As for the minimum wage, there must be precious few workers in industries under dominion jurisdiction who are not getting at least $1 an hour. In some industries under provincial jurisdiction, a minimum of $1 an hour might be hard to apply immediately; but in most provinces the legal minimum rates are preposterously low, and if parliament set a minimum of $1 for industries under its jurisdiction, that might provide a spur to provincial laggards.
I remind the government that these are the words of the Canadian Labour Congress in its brief to the cabinet on October 21, 1957, and that therefore the bill now before the House of Commons is a clear-cut implementation of that request for a minimum wage of $1 an hour enacted by the federal parliament to cover all those employees who are in works, businesses and undertakings that come under federal labour jurisdiction.
I am satisfied that there is support for the principle of a minimum wage at the federal level in the other parties in the house. It has been indicated to me by members of both of the other opposition parties that they like this legislation. Some of them have changes here or there that they might like to make, and I may say in that connection that if the bill is given second reading, as I hope it will be, I will then move that it be referred to the committee on industrial relations so that there may be public hearings about it and so that any details of the bill that members might like to have altered could be adjusted so as to meet the various viewpoints. In other words, all we are dealing with at second reading is the principle of the bill.
Of course, we could get into an argument as to what the principle is. I think the principle of the bill is that there should be established by law a legal minimum wage for employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction and that that legal minimum should be not less than $1 per hour.

speechtext: Good boy.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Not
only does the principle of this bill have the support, to my knowledge, of members in all opposition parties, but I have before me evidence that it must have the support of members on the government side of the house. I have before me a clipping reporting, by the Canadian Press, an address made by the present Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition, at Vineland, Ontario, in February of this year. It was a speech that seemed to be directed mainly to labour matters in which the then leader of the opposition promised that if his party came to power after the then ensuing election there would be a number of items of labour legislation put on the statute books. One of those items, as indicated by the then leader of the opposition at Vineland was in these words, within quotation marks, "enact legislation to provide minimum wages."
It is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister, did not just say something casually when he made that promise in February because I, too, have in my hand a copy of a document to which frequent reference has been made in this house, namely, the "Highlights of Progressive Conservative Policy", which are contained in a booklet spread far and wide in Canada during the recent election campaign. It is a document, on the front of which is that famous picture of the Prime Minister. On page 7 of the document there are quite a number of items which the Conservative party promised would be implemented if that party came to power. I find here exactly the same words that the Prime Minister used in his speech at Vineland in February. I read from page 7:
The Progressive Conservatives are convinced now, as always, that the free enterprise system coupled with effective free trade unions, offers Canadian labour the best assurance of opportunity, security and highest possible standard of living.
Then, I jump down to the point that is relevant to the bill now before us:
To attain this end we shall;
(d) Enact legislation to provide minimum wages, hours of labour, and vacations with pay for all workers under federal jurisdiction.
Well, that is quite clear. The Progressive Conservative party, like the other parties in this house, favours legislation at the

federal level to provide minimum wages for all workers under federal labour jurisdiction. Since that is the case, I hope that this house will see fit, in an hour or so, to give second reading to this bill so it might be sent, on the motion I would then make, to the committee on industrial relations.
I suppose that, despite my hope that the bill will be approved by the house, I should anticipate some of the objections that might be made and give answers to those objections even before they are presented. One objection that may, of course, be made by some- I do not know why it would but it could be made-would be that the minimum rate specified in the bill is too high, a rate of $1 an hour. The only possible reason for anyone making that objection would be, of course, that so far as I know no province yet has passed a minimum wage order that is that high. The answer to that, Mr. Speaker, has already been given to the government in the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress.
Surely, there is a place in Canada for the federal government to give leadership. The federal government cannot dictate to the provinces in matters of labour legislation. The provinces are sovereign in this field, as is the federal parliament, but a lead can be given. Surely in this day and age, at today's cost of living and in the light of today's gross national production, the suggestion that anybody should be asked to work for less than $1 an hour is ridiculous and grossly unjust. I hope that no one will seriously argue against that rate. In fact, I suspect there may be those who will criticize me for not having made the figure higher, and that is a criticism to which I would not object. I hope, nevertheless, that that is a point we might thresh out if and when the bill gets to the committee on industrial relations.
Another objection that may be offered is that the provinces that have legislation regarding minimum wages, for the most part if not entirely, provide for the rate to be fixed by the lieutenant governor in council or by some minimum wage board or in some other way than by including it right in the statute. This practice has more justification in the provinces where a much wider range of industries and kinds of work is involved. So far as federal labour jurisdiction is concerned it extends to a limited number of kinds of businesses and industries. They are set out in one of the sections of the bill. Since we know the exact categories of workers to be covered by this bill we are in a better position than the provinces are to decide what is a reasonable minimum wage.
I might point out also that there is a certain tendency on the part of some provincial
Industrial Relations
governments to crawl out from under their responsibility as to what the minimum wage should be by saying that this is for the minimum wage board or some such advisory body to decide upon. We think that in terms of responsible government it would be better to have the minimum put right into the act. I would not be averse to the act being changed to permit the governor in council, on the recommendation of some advisory body, to raise the figure higher. I think, in any case, parliament should take the responsibility of putting right in the act what the bare minimum should be.
Another objection that might be raised would be the suggestion that this bill, unlike some of the provincial measures, covers all the workers in the field covered by federal labour jurisdiction. Most of the provincial statutes pick out certain sectors of industry, some of them even make a division on geographical terms. I point out again that that is because provincial labour jurisdiction extends to just everybody who works at anything except those in the categories reserved for federal labour jurisdiction. Since that is the case, it is necessary to leave a certain amount of latitude to the lieutenant governor in council to deal with matters.
So far as federal labour jurisdiction is concerned, once we get beyond transportation, the employees in banks and in communications, there are few employees covered, so there are not so many questions about the kinds of employees who may be covered. Hence, there really is no doubt but that we have a responsibility to draft the legislation in such a way as to cover all of those who come under federal labour jurisdiction.
Another objection that might be offered, if someone is just looking for an excuse as a basis to oppose the legislation, would be that this is in advance of what the provinces have put on their statute books thus far.
I think we have already answered that in the quotation I gave from the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress. I do not apologize for this bill being in advance of what the provinces have enacted. I am proud of that fact. That is the sort of thing we should be doing in this parliament, namely giving a lead, proposing legislation that matches today's conditions.
Surely in today's conditions no one can seriously contend that the minimum wage should be anything less than this figure of $1 per hour. I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members generally will realize that this bill is in line with the position that has been taken by all parties, namely that it is time to round out our labour legislation.

Industrial Relations
Particularly I hope that hon. members on the government side will realize how fully the presentation of this bill coincides with the things they said during the election campaign with regard to labour. They promised a great deal more. In fact, from what was said during the election campaign and from what was said by government spokesmen after the new government came into office on June 21, I thought that we would have at this session a review of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and the introduction of legislation on vacations with pay, statutory holidays, maximum hours of work and minimum wages. But the Prime Minister today gets to his feet and, in reply to one question, says that it depends on the co-operation of the house whether certain measures can be brought forward. But when we come back with a supplementary question he admits that some of the matters that we want are not ready as far as the government is concerned. In other words, that excuse about the co-operation of the house becomes a hollow one when one really examines into it. I hope that excuse will not be put up in relation to this matter. When the Conservatives were on the opposition side of the house they promised for a number of years back that they would review and overhaul the labour legislation. They have stood for the principle that is contained in this bill. They said so during the election campaign. They have said so since then. This bill, Mr. Speaker, is not a bill which calls upon the federal government as such to spend any money. This is a bill which requires employers who come under federal labour jurisdiction to meet certain conditions, and it undoubtedly would result in increased costs to those employers. The bill does not specifically name the civil service or employees of crown corporations. In speaking to the bill which is presently before the house, which is a bill to provide minimum wages for employees, I wish to state at the outset that I am in wholehearted support of any measures within reason which may tend to better the lot of the wage earner be he a labourer or any other type of employee because like many other hon. members in this house I am one who has been in that particular class all his life.
I have been closely associated with labour for many years and feel that I am well aware of the problems of the employee. I have been a mine employee for the past 22 years and prior to that I worked for a long period of time in various jobs in the city of Winnipeg. If I might be permitted to dispel any doubts as to my personal experience with the problems of labour I would like to cite the following example. I have in my hand an urgent letter which I received from a national publication in this country, Maclean's magazine, which is in the process of preparing an article which I hope will shortly appear in their publication concerning the district and town of Flin Flon. This most recent letter which is one of many I have received from them lately lists a great number of questions which they have submitted for my approval, verification or correction. In bringing up this point I would like to refer to one question they have submitted for my verification or approval. They ask me to confirm that I am now a Conservative member of parliament representing the constituency of Churchill and that in the mid-thirties I earned 56 cents an hour and worked 56 hours a week in a northern Manitoba mine. That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the questions I will have to correct for Macleans Magazine because although I did work 56
Industrial Relations
hours a week my wages were not 56 cents an hour, they were 42 cents an hour at that time.
In case you might think 42 cents an hour is a fantastically low figure I would hasten to explain that one of the main reasons for my going to the northern part of Manitoba to work for that kind of money was due to the fact that it was approximately double the amount I could possibly have earned in the city of Winnipeg in those days.
During my years as a mine employee I have been a union member continuously wherever possible and when possible I acted as a union steward. I hope hon. members will realize from these remarks that I am not only very sympathetic to the problems of employees but I would like to see those problems alleviated to the greatest extent and as quickly as possible.
Many of the provisions of this bill to provide minimum wages for employees are highly commendable and well thought out and some of them would tend to lessen to an appreciable degree some of the burdens presently being shouldered by a great many employees. There are, however, certain aspects of the bill which I think should be given much more consideration.
I hope that I have convinced this house that I know partially from personal experience the problems of the working man and that I am wholeheartedly in sympathy with him. We must, however, be fair, honest and open minded about these considerations; especially so when in many cases under this bill we shall be legislating in regard to public money. In this regard, I might say that be it public or private money with which we are dealing we must have the same consideration at all times.
I am one who will always look on both sides of the fence, and despite the fact that for over 15 years I worked as a labourer or mill operator,-and I believe did a good enough job to earn my money-I still feel that I and many others owe a great deal to the mining industry of Canada. I grant that over the years shareholders and promoters have made millions of dollars, but they also- and I know this very well-provided me with an opportunity to bring up my family in an atmosphere which was the essence of security. I believe and I honestly think that that is one of the things that the working men of Canada want today. People might say, or some might think, that I should be afraid that some of my constituents might feel that I am saying these things merely to get into the good graces of a mining company. Well, the people of the Flin Flon area certainly will not say that because there are

I make no excuses for that position. There is perhaps another reason why such legislation has not been brought forward since 1935. In 1935 it was deemed necessary to put a floor under wages because we did have a Tory administration at that time and there was a natural apprehension that the bottom was going to fall out of things. It may be understandable that there is such a feeling throughout the country now and that may be one of the reasons that prompted the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to bring forward this legislation again at this time.
There should be no quarrel among hon. members regarding the setting of a floor of $1 under wages. Some service industries make use of the gratuity system in order to make up the wages of those who are required to work at very inadequate wages. This legislation may go a long way towards eradicating that type of thing and it would lead to a much greater feeling of self-respect among employees. An employee who is being paid a living wage should not and would not be looking for gratuitous assistance from those whom he is required to serve.
I remember that back in 1947 the battle cry of the miners was for a wage of $1 an hour. They thought that if they could reach such a wage they would have achieved a goal really worth striving for. Since that time, of course, wages of miners in most instances and certainly of those in other industries have more than doubled.
It is hard to visualize people in this day and age being required to give their services for anything less than $8 for eight hours work. There are precedents even in this house for the setting of a floor. I refer to farm products. For instance, does not the wheat board, a body established by parliament, set at the beginning of the crop year the minimum price that they are prepared to pay for wheat? New legislation is anticipated, in fact it is on the order paper even today, which we hope will be brought forward before the Christmas recess so that
Industrial Relations
we will be able to deal with it and give farmers producing other products some assurance that they will receive a proper price for their goods.
Therefore it is not setting a precedent for parliament to accept legislation which would establish a minimum wage of $1 an hour for all employees. The unemployment insurance commission considers that an unemployed person sitting idly by his fireside- perhaps I should not say "idly" but it is correct-is entitled to at least $30 a week, and if he is able to go out and work for a day or two a week he can have an income of $43 a week. The average work week in Canada is in some cases even less than 40 hours a week but 40 hours is more or less standard. Such an unemployed person is entitled to be idle and receive up to $43 a week. Surely a person working in a service industry or other productive industry should be entitled to at least a minimum of $40 a week.
I do not want to take any more time in this debate. I hope the bill will be voted on this afternoon and that if it is given second reading it will go to the committee on industrial relations where it may receive a thorough study and where we may be able to find out if there is in fact a large or small number of people who even at this date in 1957 are being required to work for less than $1 an hour.

This effort to establish a minimum wage act has remained dormant now for many years. I am glad that we have come a long way and, so far as I am concerned, there still may be a long way to go before we reach that Utopia that we may relegate to the land of our dreams and leave as an objective to which we can aim but an objective which we can never attain in full.
I am going to take up for a moment the relationship of this act to the majority of the people in the riding which I represent who are farmers. I am going to suggest to you that although there is no mention of farmers in the bill and it does not apply to farmers I am sure that one of the reasons behind the introduction of the bill is that the actions of this government in setting a minimum wage should have an influence on the people in the country. It should influence every employer, and it should influence all wage earners. It should influence everybody. It should set an example of fair dealing in the matter of wages.
With that in mind, I should like to point out to this house that it is out of the question for the average farmer to come anywhere near living up to the provisions of this bill. I have made a little calculation. We know that there are slightly more than 30 days in the average month, but we will take 30 days for ease of calculation. Three meals a day at 40 cents a meal would come to $1.20, and for 30 days that amounts to $36. If we allow 50 cents a day for a bed to sleep in, that would amount to another $15, and $15 added to $36 gives us a total of $51 for board and lodging which a farmer could expect to deduct from the cash remuneration he paid his hired man. Then, if we limited ourselves to working eight hours a day, and I do not know of any farmer who does because it is mostly ten hours or more, at $1 per hour this would amount to $8 a day and for 30 days it would amount to $240. We must remember that on a farm Sunday is just like most other days. Then, if we subtract $51 form $240, we arrive at $189 per month, plus board, that the average farmer would be expected to pay if he lived up to the good example set by this bill.
If anyone inquires at the unemployment insurance or labour offices, I think he will find that the average wages paid to newcomers to the country run from about $65 a month and board up to possibly $100 for those with some experience. The hired man has disappeared from the rural scene in the area which I represent. I know of two

or three hired men in the township in which I live. They are men who have worked for their employers for 25 years or 30 years. They are elderly men who can no longer depart for other places or other jobs. They are going to finish right where they are. That is the only type of help left in that area.
Last spring while I was going around campaigning I passed a field one morning and in it saw a neighbour lady. I knew her and I know her husband. Her husband is crippled up with rheumatism. I expect that both of them have been drawing old age security allowances for some years. The little old lady was out on the tractor trying to plant some oats. That is the farm situation in the area from which I come. The young people are leaving. The old folks are left struggling as best they can to keep the homes together.
I am pointing this situation out only to show that we must do something. If we are going to set minimum rates of wages and if we are going to relate rates of wages and prices, and are going to protect industry which includes both management, labour and invested capital, then I wish to point out to this house that we are also going to have to take similar action in raising the status of our farmers.
I do not know whether or not the resolution is out of order as I have no technical knowledge in that regard. I do not know that it matters very much whether it is or not. I am in favour of legislation of this kind. I hope that something can be done to improve the standard of living of those on lower rates of pay. However, we must equalize the rest of our economy so that one class of people is not discriminated against by passing legislation of this kind for the benefit of another group in our economy.

I rise at this time, Mr. Speaker, to express my sympathy for the general intention behind this bill. As I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) outline the historical background to this particular measure in this country I could not help but recall that the first minimum wage law was passed in the United States in 1938 and that its passage was possible only after a long series of court cases which finally resulted in the admission that this type of law was constitutional in Washington. It is interesting to recall that the first hourly rate established under the minimum wage law in that country was 25 cents an hour and had increased only to 40 cents an hour in 1945. When the measure was first introduced in the United States there were large numbers of employers who objected to the passage of the measure because they felt that it would have an extremely injurious effect on employment in that country. The main effect of the legislation, as experience later showed, was to displace several thousands of pecan shellers in the state of Texas and other southern states who at that time were working for eight cents an hour. Of course, the industry had to mechanize and become more efficient, so there were gains to be had on all sides.
The effect of this measure in the United States has been studied and the experience has been that it has had no harmful effect on employment opportunities, the chief difficulty being in the field of enforcement, a fact which caused difficulties to enforcement officers in the first years in the United States.
I feel that this particular measure reflects the advances that we should be making in the field of labour legislation in this country, however far they are behind those made by our neighbour to the south. For that reason I give it my support. However, I want to take the opportunity provided by the introduction of this bill to discuss some related and pertinent wage problems in my own constituency of Inverness-Richmond.
One of the hon. members of the Social Credit party asked the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre whether he could outline any employees presently receiving an hourly rate of less than $1. During the past hour or so I have been examining the wage rates now prevailing in the national parks of Canada, particularly the Cape Breton Highlands national park. I find that in that particular park there are 11 classifications of employees receiving an hourly rate of less than $1 an hour. I am sure that there are other national parks, particularly in Quebec and the maritime provinces, where classifications of employees receive an hourly rate of less than $1. I hope that the passage of this bill will have

Industrial Relations
the effect in certain instances of superseding the results that are gained from the present wage surveys conducted by the Department of Labour. At present, as hon. members are aware, these prevailing rate employees are paid according to the results of wage surveys conducted by the Department of Labour whose recommendations are then submitted to the appropriate department for action. This procedure has resulted in extremely unusual distortions and anomalies in the payment of wages to various employees in various parts of Canada. Of course the purpose of using wage surveys was a good one because an attempt was made to guarantee that government employees would receive at least the maximum average rate prevailing in any particular labour market. However, I think this particular system has serious deficiencies or at least it works well in only two particular situations.
First of all, in a situation where there is a very competitive labour market and where employers of labour are bidding for workers, with the result that the highest possible rate is paid, the wage survey table will guarantee the government rate is based on a competitive rate provided in a competitive labour market. The wage survey works well in that situation. It works well, also, in a unionized market where the action of the trade unions has guaranteed that the union rate is being observed. And then, of course, the prevailing rates to government employees is based on that type of sample.
However, in the Cape Breton Highlands national park there are very serious limitations on the use of wage surveys. I think hon. members of this house will be surprised to learn that there is a great difference in the wages paid to employees of the Cape Breton Highlands national park, for example, and the employees of the Banff national park, although both groups of workers are hired by the same employer, the government of Canada or the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. For instance, a labourer employed at the Cape Breton Highlands national park receives 70 cents an hour, while the rate for similar work in the Banff national park is $1.35. Likewise, the prevailing rate employee-the labourer in the Cape Breton Highlands national park who works a 44-hour week is paid $39.60 under the present rates, while his counterpart in the Banff national park receives $59.40, a discrepancy of almost 50 per cent in the payment made to Canadian workers employed by the same employer. For a carpenter in the Cape Breton Highlands national park, the weekly pay is $55; in Banff, it is $88. For a motor mechanic in the Cape Breton Highlands the rate is $58; in Banff

it is $74.80. The weekly rate of a painter is $48 a week in Cape Breton in respect of a 44-hour week, while in Banff it is $79.20.
I do not believe any sensible Canadian can justify this wide discrepancy which exists between these rates of pay, and members of parliament who have national parks in their constituencies, particularly in the eastern parts of Canada, should compare the wages received by their constituents with those received in other parts of the country, particularly in the western parts.
I know it is a great privilege to live on the island of Cape Breton, particularly in areas surrounding the finest and most beautiful national park in Canada, but I doubt whether employees are prepared to pay for this privilege by receiving in wage payments almost 50 per cent less, in the case of labourers, than workers in the Banff national park.
The situation is made even more absurd by the fact that wage surveys undertaken to establish the prevailing rate in this particular park are based upon a survey of wages in two fishing villages, the villages of Ingonish and Cheticamp where there is no real industrial employment and where there are no unionized plants. Even the Department of Labour would, of course, be making some improvement in its rate-setting if it took into account the wages paid to labourers in the adjacent coal mines in the Cape Breton coal field or in the steel mills in Sydney where the rates are much higher. Instead, we find the Department of Labour using these wage surveys in areas where they were never intended to apply and in which there is no basic competitive labour market or unionized market to guarantee that these workers will receive just and fair treatment.
I am supporting this measure, Mr. Speaker, as a first step toward remedying the injustice which now applies to prevailing rate employees in certain parts of Canada. I believe that its passage would guarantee to at least 11 classifications of employees in the Cape Breton Highlands national park a basic minimum of $1 an hour. I do not regard that as sufficient or proper, because I believe that these prevailing rate employees should be treated in exactly the same way as civil servants or employees of the Canadian National Railways are treated. These employees receive exactly the same rate no matter where they live in Canada. While I am supporting this measure on that ground, and for other reasons, I do not believe that the rate which would ensue under this legislation would provide fair and just treatment for these classifications of employees I have mentioned.

It is the object of this government and of this parliament to do something about narrowing the gap in income which exists between various regions of Canada. A very modest but important step would be to make the rates paid in the Highlands national park in Cape Breton equal to the highest rate applicable in Canada. Failing this, I will settle for the moment as a first step with having these 11 classifications raised to at least $1 an hour as a basic minimum.

Mr. Speaker, we presently have legislation for equal pay as between the sexes. The legislation which is presently introduced indicates a minimum wage of $1 per hour regardless of the type of work done by either of the sexes. I would like to ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) how he brings the two principles into agreement. The provinces have had control of labour legislation because of the wide differences in economic conditions across the country. Subject to an assurance that the legislation will not supersede the proper authority of the provinces and subject to an explanation regarding my first question I should like to fully support this bill.
In his introduction of the bill the hon. member referred to the universal shortening of the work week as being desirable. I feel that in relation to some industries this is questionable particularly when no consideration is given to the particular industries involved.
At the moment we have a serious problem in winter seasonal unemployment. In this connection I think it is particularly true of the western provinces where winter weather is so much more severe. This is a difficult problem for those in the agricultural industry who become unemployed but it also has another effect. Due to the large number of unemployed at that one particular time of the year we have a falling off in purchasing power right across the nation. This is inclined to create a chain reaction such as we are experiencing at the moment which then starts to create unemployment in industries across the land and produces what can develop into a serious condition of general unemployment.
What have been the original solutions adopted to meet seasonal unemployment? Much consideration has been given to this question throughout the years by unions, management, individuals and government. The first solution of course was higher wages

Industrial Relations
during the working year to compensate for lay-offs. This worked fairly well at first but gradually more people who were regularly employed were able to obtain higher wages and the unemployed person became worse off than ever before due to the increased cost of living. Another attempt made in recent years that met with some success was the promotion of winter employment and improvements in winter construction through scientific methods. This has been of particular assistance to tradesmen but is not of too much benefit to general labourers.
The basic answer to the problem on the part of the government has been unemployment insurance. This of course assisted the individual in enabling him to live during that particular period providing he qualified for receipt of benefits and the government has now acted in the face of a serious situation to improve the benefits which unemployed workers may receive at this time. This, however, does not answer the problem created by the terrific shortage of purchasing power during the winter season and it will not answer the problem facing us this winter.
The unions have recently been considering and advocating a new type of approach to this situation known as the guaranteed annual wage. In some industries which are relatively stabilized this may work and in fact in some instances the unions have been able to negotiate contracts which brought this about. Strangely enough it is not particularly new in developed countries. Some years ago when the price of tea rose sharply in Canada the reason was that the government of India had decided that the tea producers in that country should provide accommodation even if it were a mud hut and should provide food even if it were only rice to the people employed in the tea industry.
I believe that in certain industries we should direct our efforts towards shortening the work year rather than shortening working hours or the work week. This would mean a great change in thinking on the part of most concerned, away from the idea of shorter hours and a shorter work week toward a shorter working year with a paid holiday period falling in the months of January and February. This is already done in one large profession. Although they are not affected in the winter period we have long grown accustomed to acceptance of the fact that those engaged in the teaching profession receive regular pay throughout the year and we do not even think of them as being unemployed during those long periods in the summer when the schools are closed and the teachers are not doing their usual work.
A similar system could be introduced particularly for labourers in fields where
[Mr. Thompson (Edmonton-Strathcona) .1
their work cannot be accomplished or is economically unsound in the winter months. In this particular group I think it is essential that they be available for work when work is available for them and that it might be wise for them to be on paid holidays in that period when no work is available due to the fact that it simply cannot be performed or conducted at that time. This would have the effect of equalizing their pay and levelling out their purchasing power throughout the year so we would not be regularly thrown into this rise and fall in market conditions across the country.
The thought I have introduced at this time is not of course directly related to the legislation before us but it is an idea to be left before this house for those who may be interested in management, unions or the problems of government in dealing with the serious difficulties created by unemployment at a time when seasonal unemployment is of so much concern to the nation.

Mr. Speaker, representing as I do a constituency which is partly made up of working men, I could hardly do otherwise than support every measure which tends to improve the lot of these people. That is why I wish to go on record as favouring the resolution introduced by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
The main object of the bill is to provide for a basic minimum wage of $1.00 per hour for every employee coming under federal labour jurisdiction, whatever his age or ability, as long as he remains in the service of his employer, that is the government.
This bill would also authorize the governor in council to establish a higher hourly rate for part-time employees, that is for all those who work at least 32 hours a week.
This legislation is not conceived along the lines of provincial regulations regarding salaries. It constitutes a new approach to the matter and is designed to establish a minimum wage on the national level, since as yet no Canadian legislation applies in this field.
In all the provinces, minimum wage legislation (every province except Prince Edward Island has such legislation on its books) merely provides for bureaux where the rate of wages is determined after consultation with the employers and labour organizations concerned. It is generally provided that this wage must be approved by the lieutenant governor in council.

The minimum basic rates established in this way vary considerably among the various provinces and within particular provinces. The highest rates, with the exception of certain rates established for particular industries, is $30.00 a week for men in the urban centres of Alberta, and for both men and women in Saskatchewan. On the basis of a forty-hour week, this rate yields an average hourly wage of 75 cents, and on the basis of a forty-four hour week, an average of 68 cents.
It will therefore be seen that the rate proposed by bill No. 4 goes much farther than the minimum wage rates generally applied in the provinces at this time.
No province has struck a minimum general rate for all its workers. A distinction is generally made, in the provinces, between more experienced workers as well as between communities of various sizes.
Generally speaking, certain exceptions are also made with regard to certain groups of employees such as those belonging to a particular age group or those classified as apprentices.
I am sure that hon. members would find it rewarding to study provincial legislation in this regard before expressing an opinion on the matter.
In principle, this bill appears to be more along the lines of American legislation whereby a minimum wage rate of $1.00 per hour is established for employees under federal jurisdiction. This legislation was originally enacted around 1930 and provided at the time a minimum of 25 cents per hour.
One question which arises immediately is that of determining what effect that proposal would have on wages now being paid to employees who would come under the act.
According to the estimate made by the economic and research division of the Department of Labour, probably no more than 5 per cent, or approximately 20,000 employees of industries subject to federal jurisdiction are now paid less than $1.00 an hour. These are mainly to be found in a limited number of occupations such as the telephone industry, radio, transportation, grain elevators and hotels. The occupations most directly affected would be junior office employees, a certain number of telephone operators and service employees such as cleaners, watchmen, etc.
In terms of costs for the industries involved, the whole thing does not seem to be overly expensive. If this proposal were implemented, it could very well have far reaching effects on the standards of wages in the provinces. It would certainly force the provinces to increase their basic rates.
Industrial Relations
How would this proposal affect the rates paid to more experienced employees? That remains to be seen and considered.
According to available information on surveys carried out in the United States, any minimum wage legislation generally tends, in the long run, to affect salaries paid to other employees, as well as to those who come under the established minimum. By that I mean that if the lower salary ranges were increased, the higher salary ranges would be increased also.
In establishments where there are a substantial number of workers who are at present under the prescribed minimum, a large proportion of these could expect salary increases over the few months following the implementation of this legislation, a fact which would upset the economic balance of the industries concerned.
The major provisions of this bill are along the lines of a recommendation contained in a brief presented to the government by the Canadian Labour Congress on October 21 last, with regard to the establishment of a minimum wage of $1.00 per hour through legislative action.
I believe that on that occasion the representatives of the congress were informed that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) would give serious consideration to this recommendation. I think I can also say that the minister has already under consideration legislation along those lines which he will shortly bring before the house. It will be noted that the house has not been told how this basic rate of $1.00 per hour was arrived at. This matter will require more thorough consideration because of the substantial margin between that rate and the highest minimum rate provided by provincial legislation.
I think there is merit in the suggestion that this matter should be thoroughly discussed so that the house may obtain as many details as possible before coming to a decision.
While I am in favour of this bill, I would like everybody here to give the legislation serious study before arriving at any opinion in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I was surprised when my hon. friend launched the debate this afternoon to find that the ranks behind him were so thin. Indeed, all I saw over in that corner was emptiness. In view of the history of sympathy for the ranks of labour across this nation of that party I do not for a moment suggest that his absentee fellow members would not in their speeches give support to the legislation we are considering today. To

Industrial Relations
show that the Progressive Conservative party likewise have their hearts in labour and are in sympathy with the things that they were seeking and sought from the previous government so unsuccessfully. I should like to put on the record the history of our party in this regard.
The Conservative party first gave recognition to labour as far back as 1873 when they recognized the principle of fair wages and reasonable working hours. They set up the first federal machinery to promote industrial harmony between employers and employees. They gave the first recognition to compensation for employees injured at work. They appointed the first trade union member as minister of labour. They gave the first federal aid to provinces and municipalities for unemployment relief. They established the principle of unemployment insurance and set up the first national employment bureau. They established minimum wages, limitation of hours of work and fair wage contracts and, to show the country that you should never underestimate the power of a woman, in February, 1953, the Secretary of State (Mrs. Fairclough) first introduced a bill to provide equal pay for men and women in the same occupation.
She presented the bill again in November, 1953 when it received only first reading. In April, 1954 the bill was presented in the house and at that time it was voted on and defeated by a vote of 109 to 78, although several members of the previous administration supported the bill. In February, 1955 it was again defeated by a vote of 107 to 83. In January of 1956 the bill was placed on the order paper. In August, 1956 the previous administration brought the same bill in and it was passed. In that field our party forced on the previous administration, through the efforts of one of our outstanding members, legislation applicable to both sexes across the country.
Since the government has been in power it has already taken steps to combat the problems of unemployment by the very sweeping changes in the unemployment insurance benefits that were passed yesterday with the consent of all members of the house. Indeed, the government has on deck a bill to provide for statutory holidays with pay, one week in the first year of employment and two weeks thereafter.
Then to show that our interest continues in the problems of labour, a great number of whom live in my constituency of Winnipeg South, particularly in St. Vital, our party is on record that it will do all in its power to maintain full employment with the highest possible standard of living, and towards that end it has already provided indirect legislation. For example, there is the legislation to pro-

vide cash advances on farm-stored grain. That is a measure which will put in circulation a great deal of money, namely $150 million. Such money will provide additional employment and additional wages pursuant thereto for many people in western Canada.
The government has under review, and I am sure the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has made this clear, national labour legislation which they are considering in consultation with labour, management and all levels of government. Towards that end they have under consideration as well the need or lack of need for compulsory arbitration as an instrument in settling labour disputes, the elimination of delays in conciliation procedures, the limiting of hours of labour and the provision of vacations with pay for workers under federal jurisdiction, which is already on the order paper. In addition, as I have already pointed out, they have brought into the house changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act which will undoubtedly benefit a great number of people who for the time being during this temporary set-back are without employment for a longer period of time than is usual.
Therefore I think we can well be proud of the efforts that have been made by this party throughout its long and glorious history. We can assure with confidence hon. members across the way that all aspects of labour-management problems are already under consideration by the cabinet and indeed have been discussed by private members with private members and by private members with the cabinet. But you cannot build Rome in a day. We have not been encouraged by some of the antics of some of the opposition members in our desire to bring before the house as expeditiously as possible and in the interest of everyone's Christmas holidays the legislation that was set down and considered in the throne speech debate. I think it is necessary as far as members on all sides are concerned that we should move forward without any further delay to endeavour to consummate before Christmas arrives what we offered to the public of Canada before June 10.
I am one who in the practice of law has had the privilege of representing both management and labour. I represented management as an alderman of the city of Winnipeg where I was a member for three years and chairman for one year of the committee on personnel and legislation which dealt with all wage problems brought before it by the federation of civic employees. On the other side of the fence, it was my privelege to represent the firefighters of greater Winnipeg and the municipal police forces of greater

Winnipeg in their labour negotiations with management in the various municipalities surrounding our great city.

Before we rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I made brief reference to the work of the commission on the uniformity of legislation under the auspices of the Canadian Bar Association. Every year that association, meeting in convention, has done very valuable work in connection with provincial legislation in promoting uniformity of legislation with regard, for example, to acts dealing with bills of sale, chattel mortgages, and conditional sales, besides-* getting nearer to the subject-with the matter of the workmen's compensation acts of the common law provinces of our country. The commission is, no doubt, about to consider other labour legislation which is already on the statute books of the provinces, and in this useful service they are making a great contribution, without any interference by federal legislation, in this field.
I know that as late as October 21, 1957, the congress of labour submitted to the

dominion government and cabinet their memorandum on what they are seeking in the form of labour legislation from this new government, and on page 17 thereof they said in part, and I quote:
But the dominion should not confine itself to doing as well as the best of the provinces. It should give a lead. It should, specifically, establish a legal maximum work week of 40 hours and a legal minimum wage of $1 an hour. This is not really a very drastic proposal. About 65 per cent of all plant workers in manufacturing now have a standard work week of 40 hours or less; so have all railway workers and a host of others.
So, they dwell primarily on this point of a 40 hour week. However, a little later they go on to say, and I quote again:
As for the minimum wage, there must be precious few workers in industries under dominion jurisdiction who are not getting at least $1 an hour. In some industries under provincial jurisdiction a minimum of SI an hour might be hard to apply immediately, but in most provinces the legal minimum rates are preposterously low and if parliament set a minimum of $1 an hour for industries under its jurisdiction, that might provide a spur to the provincial laggards.
In its own submission, the Canadian Congress of Labour, by using the words "a minimum of $1 an hour might be hard to apply immediately" would indicate that having tapped the information available to it, the congress recognizes that there could be some difficulty in the application of federal legislation of this sort right at the outset.

depressed areas a wage rate which they in their present financial situation cannot possibly meet immediately.
Another thing which comes to mind is the question of casual employees. All of us have had some dealings with this matter in the past and have found that because of the stringent application of provincial legislation a certain hardship has been worked on people who are advanced in years, for example, and who are perhaps not able to work full time, or who, if they can work full time, cannot work to full capacity. This situation occurs when a person is suffering some physical handicap and in cases where the nature of the work is such that it can, perhaps, be done by a child, for example, but is made available to some one who requires some sort of income to supplement an old age pension.
This legislation would encroach on the supplemental earnings of many of our older citizens, and bring hardship to bear on them, because it would be necessary for the inspectors who we would have to employ under this act to prevent these people, or their employers, from engaging in this sort of relationship notwithstanding the fact that the employee might be perfectly satisfied to take less than the legal minimum of $1 because the amount he was earning did provide supplementation to a war veteran's pension or to a disabled person's pension or to an old age pension. That is a conflict which might arise if such legislation as this, or even, indeed, certain provincial legislation, were applied too stringently.
So for all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I feel that labour should be given the opportunity to follow up the brief which they submitted to the cabinet, perhaps to the industrial relations committee; make their representations, go into all the details of the possible difficulties I have endeavoured to outline, and then come forward with a well thought out act to be proposed by the government for the consideration of parliament after all these things have been thoroughly discussed and a greater degree of unanimity has been reached as to the terms and conditions to the act than is apparent at the present time.

I feel that the government should be the first to recognize it has an obligation to those over whom it has jurisdiction. The hon. member should be given an opportunity to outline to the house how many individuals might be involved and those industries to which he had particular reference in drafting the bill.
In this day and age it is unthinkable that any one should be able to pay an employee less than $1 an hour. We in this house recognize the tremendous increase in the cost of living and we found it necessary to increase the pensions of the aged, the disabled, the blind; to increase the war veterans allowance and assistance under the Old Age Assistance Act in order that the recipients of these welfare payments would be better able to meet present day costs.
The bill before us relates to individuals who are doing work in an industry whether or not it is a government-operated one. In this regard I would point out that our minimum is definitely too low. Costs are an important factor, of course, and must be borne in mind but I feel that the additional work we would get from an employee if we paid him a fair wage would be ample compensation for whatever increase might be granted.
As I listened to the hon. gentleman who introduced the bill I wondered in exactly what category temporary employees engaged by the Post Office Department would come and whether or not they would be affected by this proposed legislation. If they do come under the provisions of this bill then I would accept that as one of the reasons why we have so much difficulty at the Christmas season in securing adequate temporary help to handle the additional mail.
In crossing the country I have frequently discussed this and similar problems with those with whom I have been associated. I discovered that some of the individuals who work in our national parks receive a sum considerably less than the figure quoted in this bill. Choosing an example at random I would point out that the waitresses employed in the hotels in the national parks are dependent for a large portion of their livelihood upon the whims and fancies of philanthropic people who are prepared to reward them for their services in the way of tips which help to augment their salaries.
Recently a friend of mine who is a business executive and frequently has occasion to

Industrial Relations
travel across the country drew this very question of tipping to my attention. My friend felt that individuals receive sufficient money in the form of salary and should not be given gratuities and went on to suggest that if they did not receive a sufficient wage it should be increased so they would not be forced to rely on the philanthropic individual who is prepared to give them a few cents for the small extra services performed for him. I believe we should pay people in these circumstances a sum sufficient to enable them to live comfortably without depending on gratuities the general public might give them. The people who depend on the receipt of tips dislike being forced into the position of parasites just as much as would an employee who receives a fair wage.
I have frequently asked myself about the question of those civil servants who are not doing the jobs they should be doing. That is not just an irrelevant statement, it is a matter of fact. I am sure that hon. members in this house have frequently heard from their constituents about cases of this nature. Frequently we are told that some of our civil servants are just not doing the job they should be doing. Whether or not an individual is a civil servant and whether or not he receives $1 an hour the fact remains that if industry in the surrounding area pays more than $1 an hour or more than the wage he receives for doing a similar type of work or for the time spent in doing a specific job you have a disgruntled employee.
Naturally enough, if you are going to pay someone less than $1 an hour you are going to have an employee who is worth less than $1 an hour and if he is worth more than that sum it is reasonable to assume that the only reason he stays on the job is because he has no other job to which he can turn. In some instances he may be a person raised in an atmosphere of fear concerning the loss of his job and his inability to secure other employment. As long as such conditions exist they will not be conducive to an employer receiving from an employee the best service he can perform.
One hon. member opposite in the Liberal party mentioned that the provisions of this bill would not add to the cost of production and I would agree with him because, as I said earlier, if the present rate of pay of an employee is lower than that offered by industry in the surrounding district for comparable work the employer will not get his dollar's worth in terms of productive labour and if the employee is paid less than $1 an hour the employer will receive performance in like kind.

Mr. Speaker, when the bill was introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) he expressed the view that is common to most of us, that we are in general accord with the principle of the bill. The first time this legislation was presented was by the Bennett regime in 1934 when Canada agreed to conform to the international conventions of the League of Nations and the legislation that followed was declared ultra vires on the question of split jurisdiction. He covered the general purposes fairly well.
With respect to a minimum wage, I can recall when the matter was first introduced into and adopted by the city council of Toronto some years ago. It was more or less sponsored by James Simpson, who was active in the trades and labour councils of that day. They desired to have a minimum wage on all work pertaining to the city of Toronto. Pratically all of the labour men endorsed the idea but Jimmie Simpson pointed out that a minimum wage eventually became a maximum wage. The unions did not have the strong status they have today. Instead of calling it a minimum wage, Mr. Simpson had it accepted as a fair wage.
To see that it was enforced they had to appoint a fair wage officer and the fair wage officer was probably someone who just filled in from another department. He was not very conversant with the demands for labour at that time, and there was considerable difficulty in having the provision adhered to in the work that was being done by the various contractors for the city of Toronto. It was confirmed at that time that 50 cents an hour was the amount that should be paid to ordinary labour. Skilled labour at that time, as it is now, was generally paid a higher amount and did not come within the purview of the provision.
Then, the time came when there was unemployment. There was no unemployment insurance at that time and they had to make provision, on a welfare basis, for the people in Toronto who were out of work. That was done mainly through the removal of snow. One of the other controllers, who employed labour, conceived the idea that the way to make more work was to place more people on the snow removal and he also thought it would be a good idea to have the fair wage minimum reduced to 45 cents an hour. He was not successful in doing that; the amount of 60 cents an hour was maintained; but the point I am trying to make is that a minimum wage eventually has a tendency to become a maximum wage in the ordinary flow of lower grade workers, as I might call them.

I can remember the discussions that went on, and it was always the desire of the council to create more work. Only a certain amount of money was appropriated and when that was spent there was the usual wrangle to get more. In some winters the necessity for snow removal was not very great because there was very little snow to remove. At other times, when there were severe storms, they did not have a sufficient labour force to move the snow, and even if they did have a sufficient force they could not move it in the time required.
As the war came on they resorted to mechanical methods of removing the snow. Therefore, they reduced the labour force and they moved the snow by mechanical equipment at a considerably smaller cost.
Then there is the question of talking out this bill. Everyone who has spoken here today has said that he is in favour of the purpose and the principle of the bill; but no one is being deluded. No one can be fooled. Everyone knows that this is a case of jockeying for what might be called position. We witnessed the same performance when the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair-clough) sat on the opposition side of the house and introduced her bill calling for equal pay for female labour for equal work. We all know what happened. For three or four years in a row the matter was talked out because it was not expedient, in the eyes of the government of the day, that a bill should be brought in by a private member, because it did not give them the necessary kudos to go to the people and have to admit that some person on the side benches or in the opposition had brought in such a bill. We are in the same position. We do not intend that legislation such as this should escape us. It is covered here very amply.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was very fair in his statement today and no one can complain about that. No one can complain about his having the desire or the initiative to try to get this legislation on the statute books in his name and in the name of his party. That is fair in the hurly-burly of politics. Each one of us is striving for the ascendency of his own party.

They outlined what they desired of the government, what they approved and what they disapproved and related the hopes they had for the future. At the conclusion
